name: Anterior cerebral artery
summary: The smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid. It runs medially above the optic nerve into the interhemispheric fissure, where the anterior communicating artery links it to its partner, then arches back over the corpus callosum. Its cortical branches supply the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes as far as the parieto-occipital sulcus plus a narrow strip of the adjoining convexity, which includes the leg and foot areas of the motor and sensory cortices. Central branches, including the recurrent artery of Heubner, supply the head of the caudate and the anterior limb of the internal capsule.

anatomy.location: From the carotid terminus at the medial end of the lateral sulcus the A1 (precommunicating) segment passes over the optic nerve or chiasm to the anterior communicating artery; the A2 segment ascends in front of the lamina terminalis and genu of the corpus callosum, and the pericallosal artery (A3 onward) runs back in the callosal sulcus giving off callosomarginal and frontopolar branches.

subdivisions.name: A1 (precommunicating)
subdivisions.note: gives medial lenticulostriate perforators and the recurrent artery of Heubner near the AComm

subdivisions.name: A2 (postcommunicating)
subdivisions.note: ascends around the genu; orbitofrontal and frontopolar branches

subdivisions.name: Pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries
subdivisions.note: medial frontal and paracentral lobule, precuneus

function: Supplies the paracentral lobule (motor and sensory cortex of the contralateral leg and foot), the medial prefrontal cortex and supplementary motor area, the anterior cingulate, the anterior four-fifths of the corpus callosum, and via Heubner's artery the head of the caudate and anterior limb of the internal capsule.

bestView.label: pericallosal artery arching over the corpus callosum
paired A2 segments in the interhemispheric fissure
medial frontal cortex and paracentral lobule, the classic infarct site

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T1 the pericallosal artery is a curving flow void just above the corpus callosum; on axial slices the paired A2 segments sit in the midline in front of the genu. CTA and MRA show the A1 segments converging on the anterior communicating complex.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion along the medial frontal and parietal cortex from the frontal pole to the paracentral lobule, sometimes involving the caudate head and anterior limb of the capsule when the proximal A1/Heubner is included; bilateral when both A2s arise from one A1 (azygos variant).
pathology.timing: DWI bright within an hour; FLAIR follows by roughly 6 hours

pathology.finding: Saccular aneurysm at the A1–A2 junction; rupture gives blood in the interhemispheric fissure and frontal horns with a gyrus rectus hematoma.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI for infarction; CTA or DSA for aneurysms of the anterior communicating complex

lesionEffects.deficit: Weakness and sensory loss of the leg and foot, arm relatively spared
lesionEffects.mechanism: Paracentral lobule (leg area of the motor and sensory homunculi) on the medial surface
Medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex, especially with bilateral infarcts or a single A1 supplying both A2s
Supplementary motor area and medial frontal cortex
Supplementary motor area and its connections with Broca's area

examination: Test hip flexion and foot dorsiflexion against gravity; compare with shoulder abduction and finger extension
Check sensation on the foot and shin
Ask about bladder control and observe initiative and spontaneous speech
Elicit a grasp reflex by stroking the palm
pearls: Leg-predominant hemiparesis points to the ACA, arm and face-predominant to the MCA
Bilateral leg weakness with incontinence after subarachnoid hemorrhage suggests bilateral ACA vasospasm from an AComm aneurysm
Because Heubner's artery arises from the proximal ACA, a proximal occlusion can add a faciobrachial component via the anterior limb of the internal capsule

pitfalls: Isolated leg weakness is also seen with a parasagittal meningioma and with a spinal cord lesion; sensory level and reflexes help
ACA infarcts are much rarer than MCA infarcts and embolic sources should still be sought
